blocks.text: India's quasi-federal structure is characterized by a well- defined framework of Centre-State relations, designed to maintain a balance between a strong central authority and autonomous state governments.
Sarkaria Commission: 1983
Suggested reforms to strengthen cooperative federalism.
Strong Centre: Retained a strong Union while ensuring States' autonomy.
Article 356: To be used sparingly and only as a last resort.
Governor's Role: Should be a neutral figure, not involved in active politics of the State.

Inter-State Council (1990): Examined Centre—State relations and emphasized the need for better coordination between the Union and States, recommended the creation of the Inter-State Council under Article 263 of the Constitution. Based on this recommendation, the Inter-State Council was established in 1990.
All India Services: Favoured their continuation for administrative uniformity.
Financial Relations: Suggested fair distribution of resources and greater consultation with States.
Concurrent list: Centre should consult States before making laws on subjects in this list.
Punchhi Commission: 2007
Suggested reforms for better federal balance.
Governor's Role: Fixed tenure; should act as an impartial constitutional authority.
If bill is reserved for the President, it should be disposed of within six months to avoid unnecessary delays in the legislative process.
Rajmannar Commission: 1969 (setup by Tamil Nadu govt.)
Articles related to centre-state relations:
Legislative Articles 245-255

SSEEO KS Division of legislative powers between Parliament and State legislatures Procedures for passing joint legislation Administrative · Articles 256-263 SOROS Coordination between Parliament and State legislatures in the implementation of laws and policies Financial Articles 268-293 Relations Distribution of financial resources between the Centre and States Mechanisms for intergovernmental transfers Legislative Relations (Part XI, Articles 245-255):
Article 245: Extent of laws made by Parliament and State Legislatures.
Article 246: Subject matter of laws (Seventh Schedule - Union, State, Concurrent Lists)
246A: Allows states to legislate on inter-state supply of goods & services.
Article 247: Power of parliament to provide for the establishment of certain additional courts.
Article 248: Grants Parliament exclusive power to make laws, including taxation, on any matter not listed in the Concurrent or State Lists (residuary powers).
Article 249: Power of Parliament to legislate with respect to matter in the state list in the national interest.
Article 250: Power of Parliament to legislate if a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation.
Article 251: If a State law conflicts with a Parliament law made under Articles 249 or 250, the Parliament law prevails and the State law becomes void to the extent of inconsistency.
Article 252: Parliament can make law on state subjects if two or more states request.
Article 253: Legislation to give effect to international agreements.
Article 254: Establishes the "doctrine of repugnancy"
to resolve conflicts between central and state laws on Concurrent List subjects.
254(2): A state law repugnant to a central law can prevail in the state only if it is reserved for the President's consideration and gets his assent.
Article 255: If prior recommendation or sanction (e.g., of the President or Governor) is required for a law but not obtained, the law is not invalid if such assent is given later.
Administrative Relations (Part XI, Articles 256-263):
Article 256: Obligation of States and the Union to ensure compliance with parliamentary laws.
Article 257: Control of the Union over States in certain cases (ensuring no impediments to Union executive power, protection of railways).
Article 258: Power of the Union to confer powers on States.
Article 259: The President may entrust functions of the Union to the State Government in certain cases.
Article 260: The Government of India may, by agreement, undertake functions in territories outside India.
Article 261: Public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of the Constitution of India shall be recognized and respected throughout India.
Article 262: Adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-state rivers.
Article 263: Provisions with respect to an inter-state Council. irinancial Relations (Part XII, Articles 268-293):
Article 270: Taxes levied and collected by the Union and distributed between the Union and the States.
Article 271: Surcharge on certain taxes for purposes of the Union.
Other related articles:
Article 302: The Indian Parliament is empowered to impose restrictions on trade, commerce, and intercourse within India.
Inter-State Council (ISC) - 1990
It was established on the recommendation of Sarkaria Commission.
Article 263 of the Indian Constitution establishes the Inter- State Council (ISC) to address inter-State issues and foster harmonious relations between the States and the Union.
Composition of the Inter-State Council: Chairman: Prime Minister
Members: Chief Ministers of all States
Chief Ministers of Union Territories with Legislative Assemblies
Administrators of Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies
Six Union Cabinet Rank Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister of India.
Zonal Councils are the statutory (and not the constitutional) bodies.
They are established by an Act of the Parliament States Reorganisation Act of 1956.

The act divided the country into five zones- Northern > HQ-Delhi Southern — HQ-Chennai Central -— HQ-Allahabad/Prayagraj Eastern — HQ-Kolkata Western — HQ-Mumbai and provided a zonal council for each zone.
Composition of the Zonal Council: Chairman: Union Home Minister
Vice Chairman: Chief Ministers of the States included in each zone act as Vice-Chairman for that zone by rotation, each holding office for a period of one year at a time.
